title: What Is Allied Health? A Guide to 20 Allied Health Careers
summary: Allied health includes 200+ healthcare professions. Compare 20 allied health careers by pay, training time, and job outlook, and see how to get started.
body_markdown:
When people think about[healthcare careers](https://www.stepful.com/post/jobs-in-healthcare-medical-field) , they often think first of doctors, nurses, and dentists. But many other important healthcare roles help patients every day. The majority of these fall under the umbrella of allied health.


The Association of Schools Advancing Health Professions (ASAHP) counts more than 200 distinct professions in this category, employing roughly[12 million people](https://www.asahp.org/what-is) in the United States.


Allied health professionals are trained to help diagnose health problems, provide treatment, support recovery, help people stay healthy, and/or improve healthcare services. These are good-paying,[in-demand jobs](https://www.stepful.com/post/most-in-demand-medical-jobs) that help both people and communities.


Training can range from a few months of coursework to an advanced degree. A phlebotomist who trained for a month and a speech-language pathologist with a master's degree are both allied health professionals.


This guide explains what allied health means and profiles 20 common allied health professions and a set of more specialized roles. We’ll talk about why these careers are in demand and how to get started.


## What Is Allied Health?


The[ASAHP and the federal government](https://www.asahp.org/what-is) each have their own definition of allied health, but they generally look like this:


Allied health is the broad group of healthcare professions distinct from medicine and nursing, whose members use evidence-based practice for diagnosis, evaluation, treatment, disease prevention, wellness, and health systems administration.


In general, these health professionals do not hold a doctoral-level degree in medicine, dentistry, pharmacy, public health, chiropractic, clinical psychology, social work, or counseling.


Instead, they are trained professionals, often certified and licensed, with some holding advanced degrees. Education requirements vary widely across these careers.


An optician can start with a high school diploma and get on-the-job training. An athletic trainer needs a master's degree and, in nearly every state, a license.


Don’t be intimidated by the mention of advanced degrees. A high school diploma or GED can make you eligible for many[entry-level healthcare jobs](https://www.stepful.com/post/entry-level-healthcare-jobs) or training programs. Other programs require college coursework or a prior degree.

[Take the Quiz!](https://www.stepful.com/healthcare-career-quiz)


### How Allied Health Differs From Nursing and Medicine


Physicians (MDs and DOs) diagnose disease and direct the overall course of treatment. After college, they do four years of medical school plus three to seven years of residency.


Registered nurses (RNs) coordinate and deliver ongoing patient care across an entire treatment plan. They typically have an associate or bachelor's degree in nursing and an RN license.


Allied health professionals typically work within a specific technical, therapeutic, or administrative specialty. They work alongside doctors, nurses, and dentists to support patient care.


A radiology tech produces the X-ray images a physician reads. A respiratory therapist manages the ventilator that keeps a patient breathing. A medical assistant helps with clinical and administrative tasks in a clinic or doctor’s office.


## List of Allied Health Professions


Allied health includes more than 200 distinct professions, far more than any single article can cover. The 20 careers below illustrate the range of allied health opportunities, and together they account for millions of jobs.


Most pay and employment figures come from the[U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)](https://data.bls.gov/oesprofile/) and reflect May 2025 wage data. If you're mostly interested in salaries, check out our guide to the[highest-paying allied health careers](https://www.stepful.com/post/highest-paying-allied-health-careers) .


Job growth outlook is the BLS projection for how much total employment in that occupation will change from 2025 to 2035. For context, the BLS projects a 3% growth rate across all occupations during that decade.

### 1) Medical Assistant


[Medical assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-medical-assistant) (MAs) do both clinical and administrative tasks. They can take a patient’s vital signs and prep them for an exam or schedule an appointment and update medical records.[They work mostly in](https://www.stepful.com/post/where-do-medical-assistants-work) physicians' offices, outpatient clinics, and hospitals.


Stepful’s[Online Medical Assistant Program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant) takes five months to complete and includes two live, 90-minute classes per week. The program prepares students to earn the National Healthcareer Association’s Certified Clinical Medical Assistant (CCMA) credential.


- **Median pay:**[$44,304 per year, $21.30 per hour](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant-salaries/united-states)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 833,900
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 13% growth, much faster than average
- ‍ **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED. Most employers prefer training and certification. Training can take from five months to two years for degree programs.


[Learn about Stepful's 5-Month Online Medical Assistant Program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant)


[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/medical-assistant)


### 2) Pharmacy Technician


[Pharmacy technicians](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-pharmacy-technician) help fill and label prescriptions, measure medication, manage inventory, and process insurance claims under a pharmacist's supervision. About half work in retail pharmacies, but they can also work in hospitals. You may need to be licensed in some states.


Stepful’s[Pharmacy Technician Professional](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-technician-professional) program prepares you for certification and is ASHP/ACPE-accredited in some states. The coursework is 100% online and is followed by mandatory, in-person clinical hours.


- **Median pay:**[$44,054 per year, $21.18 per hour](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-technician-salaries/united-states) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 471,200 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 6% growth, faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED and training (on-the-job or through a program). Most employers prefer certification. Requirements vary by state, so check your state board of pharmacy.


[Learn about Stepful's 4-Month Online Pharmacy Technician Program](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-tech)


[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/pharmacy-tech)


### 3) Dental Assistant


[Dental assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-dental-assistant-what-do-they-do) prepare patients and instruments, hand tools to the dentist during procedures, take X-rays where state rules allow, and more. About 91% work in dentists' offices. Schedules vary, and some dental assistants work evenings or weekends.


Each state has its own requirements in terms of training, certification, and licensing. Stepful’s[Certified Dental Assistant](https://www.stepful.com/dental-assistant) program takes four months to complete and prepares students for the Dental Assisting National Board's Radiation Health and Safety (RHS) exam.


- **Median pay:**[$48,070 per year, $23.11 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-assistants.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 388,600
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 7% growth, much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** Requirements vary by state. Some states require an accredited dental assisting program and an exam; others allow on-the-job training. Many certificate programs take four months to a year and may combine online coursework with hands-on training. Check your state requirements.


[Learn about Stepful's Online Dental Assistant Program](https://www.stepful.com/dental-assistant)


[Explore Program](https://www.stepful.com/dental-assistant)


### 4) Clinical Laboratory Technologist & Technician


Lab techs perform the lab tests needed for diagnosing, treating, and preventing disease. Technologists perform more complex tests and procedures, while technicians handle routine testing under supervision. These results are critical to a patient’s treatment plan.


- **Median pay:**[$62,930 per year, $30.26 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/clinical-laboratory-technologists-and-technicians.htm) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 343,000 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 3% growth, average **‍**
- **Education required:** A bachelor's degree in medical technology for technologists; technicians can qualify with an associate degree in clinical laboratory science. Some states require certification for licensing or registration.


### 5) EMT and Paramedic


EMTs and paramedics respond to 911 calls. They must assess and stabilize patients under pressure, then transport them to hospitals. EMTs provide basic life support after a certificate program that takes under a year.


Paramedics complete significantly more training and can administer medications, interpret EKGs, and perform advanced airway procedures. Their training programs vary in length and include supervised field experience.


- **Median pay:**[$44,470 per year for EMTs and $60,600 for paramedics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/emts-and-paramedics.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:**[181,900 EMTs and 102,200 paramedics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/emts-and-paramedics.htm#tab-3)
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 6% growth, faster than average
- **Education required:** EMTs need a high school diploma or GED and a certificate training program. Paramedics complete an approved paramedic education program, which may award a certificate, associate degree, or bachelor’s degree. All states require EMTs and paramedics to be licensed; most require[National Registry](https://www.nremt.org/EMT/Certification) certification.


### 6) Radiology Technologist


[Radiology technologists](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-radiology-tech) , or rad techs, position patients and operate X-ray, CT, and fluoroscopy equipment to produce the images doctors need to diagnose injuries and illnesses. They can also specialize in imaging methods like mammography or CT, or pursue additional training in MRI.


Most states require radiology techs to be licensed or certified. Regardless of state requirements, most employers prefer to hire certified techs.


Stepful's[Radiology Tech Program page](https://www.stepful.com/training/radiology-tech) provides information about the training and career support. To become a certified radiologic technologist, you must complete the required coursework and clinical training before taking the ARRT certification exam.


- **Median pay:**[$80,110 per year, $38.52 per hour](https://www.stepful.com/post/radiology-tech-salary) ; MRI and other specialty techs earn more **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 234,200 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 5% growth, faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** You need a high school diploma or GED to begin training. Certification requires a two-year or four-year degree. State licensing is required in most states.


### 7) Dental Hygienist


[Dental hygienists’](https://www.stepful.com/post/dental-assistant-vs-dental-hygienist) primary job is cleaning teeth. They also screen for oral disease, take X-rays, and coach patients on oral health. About[94% work in dental offices](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-hygienists.htm#tab-3) , and many work part-time. This job has flexibility and is the highest-paying on this list.


- **Median pay:**[$98,100 per year, $47.16 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-hygienists.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 225,300
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 8% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** You need at least an associate degree in dental hygiene, which typically takes about three years. Every state requires hygienists to be licensed, and requirements vary by state.


### 8) Medical Records Specialist


Medical records specialists organize and maintain patient health information. Some specialize in medical coding, assigning codes used for billing and reimbursement. It's one of the few allied health roles with little to no patient contact.


Medical billing and coding programs include training in electronic health records, coding systems, and privacy laws.


- **Median pay:**[$51,140 per year, $24.59 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 200,700 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 8% growth, much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED is enough to qualify, but most employers prefer or require training and certification. There are 2-year and 4-year degree options for this field as well.


### 9) Speech-Language Pathologist


Speech-language pathologists evaluate and treat communication and swallowing disorders. They may help kids with speech delays or stroke patients relearning how to eat. They work in schools, hospitals, rehab facilities, and private clinics. It's the second highest-paying role on this list.


- **Median pay:**[$97,870 per year, $47.05 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/speech-language-pathologists.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 193,400
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 17% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** A master's degree in speech-language pathology plus a license in every state.


### 10) Phlebotomist


[Phlebotomy](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-is-a-phlebotomist-and-what-do-they-do) is one of the easiest[entry-level healthcare jobs](https://www.stepful.com/post/entry-level-healthcare-jobs) to get into. Phlebotomists draw blood for testing, transfusions, research, and donation, then label and log the samples.


When choosing a program, compare[length](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-it-take-to-become-a-phlebotomist) ,[cost](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-much-do-phlebotomy-classes-certification-cost) , and hands-on training requirements.


- **Median pay:**[$45,230 per year, $21.75 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/phlebotomists.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 143,900
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 7% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** You only need a high school diploma or GED and a short training program to get started. Some employers may even train on the job. However, some states may require certification and licensing.


### 11) Respiratory Therapist


About 80% of respiratory therapists work in hospitals caring for patients who can't breathe well on their own. They work with patients who have asthma and COPD and those who are on ventilators in the ICU. They run diagnostic tests, manage patients’ ventilators, and teach patients to use equipment at home.


- **Median pay:**[$82,280 per year, $39.56 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/respiratory-therapists.htm) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 142,000 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 9% growth, much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** An associate degree, plus a[license in every state except Alaska](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/respiratory-therapists.htm#tab-4) .


### 12) Surgical Technologist


[Surgical technologists](https://www.stepful.com/post/what-surgical-techs-do-duties-responsibilities) set up the operating room, sterilize and organize instruments, and pass tools to the surgeon during operations.


- **Median pay:**[$64,650 per year, $31.08 per hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/surgical-technologists.htm#tab-1) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:**[118,400](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/surgical-technologists.htm#tab-3) **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 5% growth, faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** A certificate program or an associate degree with certification preferred by employers.


[Learn about Stepful's 4-Month Online Surgical Tech Program](https://www.stepful.com/surgical-tech)[Learn more](https://www.stepful.com/surgical-tech)


### 13) Physical Therapist Assistant


As the fastest-growing profession on the list, physical therapist assistants deliver the hands-on treatment a physical therapist prescribes, guide exercises, and apply manual therapy. They can also use ultrasound and stimulation, and they track how patients progress.


- **Median pay:**[$68,380 per year, $32.88 per hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/physical-therapist-assistants-and-aides.htm#tab-5) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:**[114,100](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/physical-therapist-assistants-and-aides.htm#tab-6) **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 23%, much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** An associate degree from an accredited program (required in all states), plus licensure or certification.


### 14) Massage Therapist


Massage therapists treat soft-tissue pain and tension in clinics, spas, chiropractic offices, hospitals, and private practices. Many therapists are self-employed and set their own hours, which makes this an attractive job for someone who needs work flexibility.


- **Median pay:**[$58,450 per year, $28.10 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/massage-therapists.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 155,400
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 15% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED and a certificate training program. Most states require a state license or registration.


### 15) Diagnostic Medical Sonographer


Ultrasounds are used for many conditions and are common in prenatal care. Sonographers run the equipment and capture the images that physicians need to assess and diagnose medical conditions.


- **Median pay:**[$96,590 per year, $46.44 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/diagnostic-medical-sonographers.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 92,200
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 14% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED plus a certificate training program or an associate degree. Some states require certification or licensing.


### 16) Dietitian and Nutritionist


Dietitians work in hospitals, long-term care facilities, outpatient clinics, and schools and public health programs. Many have their own private practices. They assess nutritional needs, create meal plans, and counsel patients managing diabetes, eating disorders, recovery from surgery, and many other conditions.


- **Median pay:**[$76,400 per year, $36.73 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dietitians-and-nutritionists.htm) **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 86,300 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 8% growth, much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** New candidates for[the Registered Dietitian Nutritionist](https://www.cdrnet.org/rdn) (RDN) credential need a graduate degree, required dietetics coursework, and supervised training before taking the registration exam. Many states require a license. Requirements for nutritionists vary by state and credential.


### 17) Optician


Opticians fit customers for eyeglasses and contact lenses, help them choose frames, write lab orders, and repair eyewear. Most work in optometrists' offices or retail settings. Some states require a license and an associate degree or certificate program.


- **Median pay:**[$47,260 per year, $22.72 an hour](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/opticians-dispensing.htm)
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 74,300
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 4% growth, about as fast as average
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED plus on-the-job training. Some states require a license, which may require an associate degree, an approved program, or supervised experience.


### 18) EKG Technician


EKG technicians have a focused technical skill with a short learning curve. They hook patients up to electrocardiogram equipment, run the test, and prepare the report for a physician. They must know how to correctly place the monitoring leads to get an accurate picture of the heart.


Most employers prefer certified technicians. To be eligible for the NHA's[Certified EKG Technician](https://www.nhanow.com/certification/nha-certifications/certified-ekg-technician-%28cet%29) credential, you generally need a high school diploma or GED plus an EKG training program completed within the past five years, or one year of supervised EKG work in the last three years, or two years in the last five. You must also provide evidence that you have successfully performed at least 10 EKGs on live individuals.


- **Average base pay:**[$25.26 per hour](https://www.indeed.com/career/ekg-technician/salaries) , according to Indeed’s Sept. 21, 2026, update, or about $52,541 per year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 64,500, for the broader cardiovascular technologist and technician occupation
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:**[4% growth](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/cardiovascular-technologists-and-technicians.htm#tab-6) , about as fast as average, for the broader cardiovascular technologist and technician occupation **‍**
- **Education required:** A high school diploma or GED. Certificate programs generally run a few weeks to a few months.


### 19) Occupational Therapy Assistant


One of the fastest-growing jobs in healthcare, occupational therapy assistants help patients regain the ability to do everyday tasks, like dressing, cooking, and more, after injury, illness, or disability. They carry out the treatment plan an occupational therapist designs.


- **Median pay:**[$72,300 per year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/occupational-therapy-assistants-and-aides.htm) , or about $34.76 per hour **‍**
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 52,200 **‍**
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:**[21% growth](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/occupational-therapy-assistants-and-aides.htm#tab-6) , much faster than average **‍**
- **Education required:** You need an associate degree from an accredited program and, in most cases, a state license.


### 20) Athletic Trainer


About 40% of athletic trainers work in education, at schools and colleges, but they can also work in hospitals and clinics. Athletic trainers prevent, evaluate, and treat muscle and bone injuries. Trainers now need a master's degree, and nearly all states require licensure or certification.


- **Median pay:**[$62,520 per year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/athletic-trainers.htm) , or about $30.06 per hour
- **Number of jobs in the U.S.:** 35,200
- **Job outlook, 2025-35:** 13% growth, much faster than average
- **Education required:** A master's degree, plus licensure or certification in nearly every state.

## Other Allied Health Professions


Beyond the 20 careers above, allied health includes dozens of more specialized roles, several of which pay very well and are hard to staff. If none of the professions above fit, one of these might.


- **Audiologist:** Diagnoses and treats hearing and balance disorders, and fits hearing aids and cochlear implants
- **Occupational Therapist:** Designs and directs treatment that helps patients regain the ability to perform daily activities
- **Physical Therapist:** Evaluates and treats movement problems caused by injury, illness, or disability
- **Radiation Therapist:** Delivers targeted radiation treatments to cancer patients using linear accelerators
- **Nuclear Medicine Technologist:** Prepares and administers radioactive drugs, then images how they move through the body
- **Renal Dialysis Technologist:** Sets up and monitors dialysis machines for patients with kidney failure
- **Anesthesia Technician:** Prepares, calibrates, and troubleshoots the equipment an anesthesia team relies on
- **Anesthesiologist Assistant:** Delivers anesthesia care under the direction of an anesthesiologist
- **Pathologist's Assistant:** Prepares and dissects surgical and autopsy specimens for a pathologist to examine
- **Orthotist/Prosthetist:** Designs and fits braces, supports, and artificial limbs
- **Recreational Therapist:** Uses activities like arts, games, and outings to improve patients' physical and emotional function
- **Rehabilitation Counselor:** Helps people with disabilities live independently and find and keep employment
- **Exercise Physiologist:** Builds exercise programs for patients recovering from or managing chronic disease
- **Genetic Counselor:** Assesses inherited disease risk and helps families interpret genetic test results
- **Art Therapist:** Uses art-making as a clinical tool for patients working through trauma, illness, or mental health conditions
- **Music Therapist:** Uses music and musical activity to address physical, cognitive, and emotional goals
- **Dental Laboratory Technician:** Fabricates crowns, bridges, dentures, and other dental appliances from a dentist's specifications


## Why Choose a Career in Allied Health?


Most allied health jobs pay more than the national median wage, and most of them don't require a four-year degree.


Allied health professionals work in a wide range of settings, with many different work styles. You can work directly with patients at the bedside, in a lab, or keep a desk job with little to no patient contact.


### Job Outlook and Demand


Healthcare is projected to grow much faster than the average for all occupations from 2025 to 2035, with about[1.9 million openings per year](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/home.htm) across healthcare occupations.


Some allied health professions are growing far faster than that average. Physical therapist assistants are projected to grow 23% over the decade and occupational therapy assistants 21%. Speech-language pathologists follow at 17%, massage therapists at 15%, and diagnostic medical sonographers at 14%.


This growth is driven by an aging U.S. population that will need more healthcare in the next decade. Demand will grow for imaging, rehab, lab work, and chronic disease management. At the same time, many workers will be retiring.


[HRSA's health workforce analysis](https://bhw.hrsa.gov/health-workforce-analysis/research/projections/allied-health-workforce-projections) projects shortages by 2038 in several allied health fields, including about 12,770 respiratory therapists and 43,490 opticians. These projected shortages suggest continued demand in those fields, although pay varies by role, employer, and location.


### What Allied Health Professionals Earn


Pay in allied health ranges from decent to very good. Even in entry-level jobs, the reliability of having steady work, often with good benefits, can make the lower salary more attractive.


In this field, wage levels track fairly closely with the time it takes to train for the job. However, there are some exceptions. Dental hygienists typically complete an associate degree program that takes about three years. Their median salary of $98,100 is higher than that of dietitians ($76,400) and slightly higher than that of speech-language pathologists ($97,870).


Some high-paying roles require only two-year degrees. Radiology techs ($80,110), respiratory therapists ($82,280), and diagnostic medical sonographers ($96,590) all require roughly two years of schooling and pay well above the national median wage for all occupations.


Entry-level wages are lower, but these roles can serve as stepping stones to higher-paying careers. Medical assistants ($44,304), dental assistants ($48,070), and EKG techs ($52,541 in annualized average pay) gain valuable clinical experience that can help them move into higher-level jobs with additional credentialing.


## How to Start a Career in Allied Health


With so many different careers in this category, it makes sense that there are many different career paths. The good news is that because these roles are in demand, many training options and strong support from healthcare employers and government agencies are available.


### Education and Certification Paths


[Certificate programs](https://www.stepful.com/post/online-medical-healthcare-certification-programs) are the fastest route into allied health careers. These are offered by online providers and many community colleges. Some take only a few weeks, like the phlebotomy program. Some take a few months,[like the medical assistant program](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-a-medical-assisting-program-last) .


These programs typically award a certificate of completion rather than a degree and may prepare you for a separate national certification exam.


**Associate degree programs** take about two years and open the door to higher-paying roles, like radiology technologist, respiratory therapist, diagnostic medical sonographer, and physical and occupational therapy assistant. Dental hygiene takes closer to three years.


Several roles we covered, like surgical tech, require either a certificate program or an associate degree. When you have a choice, think about your long-term goals. If you plan to pursue a bachelor’s degree later, an associate degree may provide credits toward it, depending on the school’s transfer policies and program requirements.


**Bachelor's and graduate degrees** are required for a smaller set of professions. Clinical laboratory technologists usually need a bachelor's degree. New candidates for the RDN credential need a graduate degree plus required coursework and supervised training. Speech-language pathologists and athletic trainers need a master's degree. These will be found at colleges and universities.


Licensing and registration are separate from education and vary by both role and state. Some professions require a license in all 50 states; others require it in only a handful. Check your state's licensing board before you enroll in training to make sure that program satisfies your state's requirements.

### Choosing a Training Program


When you start researching one of these careers, you’ll find a lot of training options. Here are some of the practical factors that can help you sort them out:


- Total cost, including materials and exam fees
- How long the program takes to complete
- Whether classes are[live or self-paced](https://www.stepful.com/post/self-paced-medical-assistant-program)
- Whether part-time, weekend, or[night classes](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-programs-with-night-classes) are available
- What job support you get after graduation


See if the program keeps in touch after graduation. Some[healthcare programs](https://www.stepful.com/programs) provide career support like help with your job search, resume and interview prep, and even ongoing career mentoring.


Research whether the program includes clinical hours. Some programs require an externship or hands-on clinical experience. Others have no in-person component. If the job you want requires hands-on experience, you’ll want to make sure your program supports you in getting it.


Another important factor in choosing among programs is the program's professional affiliation or accreditation. If a program isn't recognized by the credentialing body for that profession, you may not be eligible to sit for the certification exam.


And, finally, paying for the program is usually the biggest stress on students’ minds. ## What Is Allied Health FAQs


### What is allied health?


Allied health includes more than 200 professions outside medicine, nursing, and dentistry that support patient care.


It makes up[60% of the U.S. healthcare workforce](https://www.asahp.org/what-is) , with jobs like medical assistants, pharmacy technicians, dental assistants, respiratory therapists, radiology techs, and more.


Education requirements range from brief certificate programs to doctoral degrees, depending on the profession.


### What is the difference between allied health and nursing?


Registered nurses (RNs) coordinate and provide patient care across an entire treatment plan. They typically have an associate or bachelor's degree in nursing and an RN license.


Allied health professionals generally work within a specific technical, therapeutic, or administrative specialty. They work together on the same healthcare teams.


### Do all allied health careers require a college degree?


Not all do. Some roles offer certificate or on-the-job training pathways, while others require college degrees.


You can enter roles[like medical assistant](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-education-requirements) ,[pharmacy tech](https://www.stepful.com/post/pharmacy-technician-requirements) ,[dental assistant](https://www.stepful.com/post/dental-assistant-requirements-by-state) , phlebotomist, medical records specialist, and optician[without a college degree](https://www.stepful.com/post/healthcare-jobs-that-dont-require-a-college-degree) , though training and state requirements vary.


Roles like respiratory therapist and speech-language pathologist require degrees.


### What is the fastest way to start a career in allied health?


Some[phlebotomy](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-it-take-to-become-a-phlebotomist) and EKG training programs take[only weeks or months](https://www.stepful.com/post/quickest-easiest-healthcare-certifications) . Optician training varies and may involve a longer period of supervised on-the-job training.[Medical assistant](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-a-medical-assisting-program-last) ,[pharmacy technician](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-it-takes-to-become-a-pharmacy-technician-length-of-school-training) , and[dental assistant](https://www.stepful.com/post/how-long-does-it-take-to-become-a-dental-assistant) programs often take roughly four to 12 months.


### Is allied health a good career choice?


Yes. Most allied health jobs pay more than the national median wage, and most of them don't require a four-year degree.


Overall, healthcare employment is projected to[grow much faster](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/home.htm) than average, although growth varies by occupation. These jobs are also available in a wide range of settings and include many different work styles.


### What are the highest-paying allied health careers?


Among the 20 professions profiled above,[dental hygienists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-hygienists.htm) lead at a median salary of $98,100 per year, followed by[speech-language pathologists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/speech-language-pathologists.htm) at $97,870 and[diagnostic medical sonographers](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/diagnostic-medical-sonographers.htm) at $96,590.


Wages vary by geographic location and employer, so it’s always a good idea to check job listings in your area to see starting salaries.


### Which allied health jobs are growing fastest?


Among the 20 professions profiled above, physical therapist assistants have the[fastest job growth rate](https://www.stepful.com/post/fastest-growing-healthcare-jobs) predicted by the BLS at[23%](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/physical-therapist-assistants-and-aides.htm#tab-6) . Occupational therapy assistants follow at[21%](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/occupational-therapy-assistants-and-aides.htm#tab-6) , speech-language pathologists at[17%](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/speech-language-pathologists.htm) , and massage therapists at[15%](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/massage-therapists.htm) .


### Can I train for an allied health career online?


For some careers, yes. Coursework for roles like medical assistant, pharmacy technician, and medical billing and coding is widely available online.


Most clinical roles still require in-person hands-on hours before you start the job. That might be in a lab or in an externship, so check what your career requires before enrolling in a program.


### Can I move up from an entry-level allied health role?


Yes, and it's common. Sometimes, you need more school, and other times, you just need a special certification.[Medical assistants often advance](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-career-path-advancement-opportunities) to[registered nurses](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-to-registered-nurse) ,[physician assistants](https://www.stepful.com/post/medical-assistant-to-physician-assistant) , or health info techs.


Many healthcare employers help pay for the additional credentialing because they need to fill those higher-level roles.
